 San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria delivers the State of the City Address, Thursday, Jan. 15, 2026. / Zoë Meyers for Voice of San Diego 
 Sign up for The Morning Report  with all your must-read news for the day .
 Mayor Todd Gloria says he is now willing to allow Flock to go down without a fight. 
 In recent weeks, two councilmembers have crossed over to the anti-Flock side. 
 Last month, Councilmember Stephen Whitburn announced he was the newest supporter of cancelling the city’s contract with the controversial surveillance tech firm. The announcement shifted the power balance and spurred the Council to take its first step toward killing the sprawling network of automated license plate readers. 
 Still, that new majority faced one major hurdle: a potential veto from Gloria. To override the veto, they’d need six votes. They had only five. 
 Last week, the equation shifted again. Councilmember Raul Campillo announced he was changing his position. Campillo was bothered that SDPD had used Flock to surveil its own officers and, in one troubling case, a domestic violence survivor . 
 Now, Gloria says that if the Council votes to cancel the contract at its Monday meeting, he won’t veto the effort. Flock has been a useful crime fighting tool, Gloria said in a statement, but it has “clearly lost public trust.” 
 “At a time when each taxpayer dollar matters, every city investment has to justify itself. That means delivering public safety value, operating with strong accountability and maintaining the trust of the people who are paying for it,” he said.
 Public Power in San Diego Gets Renewed Push 
 Some San Diego politicians want to keep the option of ditching San Diego Gas and Electric for public, municipal-owned power alive. 
 Last week the City Council’s Environment Committee approved a resolution that would enshrine the city’s ambition to pursue a publicly-run energy grid. Councilmembers Joe LaCava and Sean Elo-Rivera voted for the resolution, while the committee’s third member Councilmember Jen Campbell voted against it. 
 Campbell was worried the city couldn’t afford to take on a grid worth billions of dollars while it struggled to overcome a budget deficit. Elo-Rivera said the math can work. 
 “When you remove one billion dollars in profit and tens of millions in executive pay, it becomes easy to see how the formula could work for San Diegans,” Elo-Rivera said during the meeting. 
 Proponents of public power failed to put the option before voters a few years ago. Then Elo-Rivera cited a lack of labor support . Some labor groups still don’t support the idea of public power. 
 “We stand firmly against any efforts to municipalize San Diego Gas and Electric,” said Nate Fairman, business manager of the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers Local 465. “We don’t trust the city government to take over the utility grid.”
 Isaiah Glasoe, program director for the advocacy group Public Power San Diego, said the public power agency wouldn’t be run by the city or a city department. He said it would likely operate with an independent board staffed with technical experts, public members and labor representation. 
 “The option is to have a billion dollars in wealth leaving San Diego or invested in San Diego,” he said. 
 Now the resolution moves to the full City Council. 
 Terra Lawson Remer + Surfboard = Podcast 
 San Diego County Board of Supervisors Chair Terra Lawson-Remer speaks at the press conference discussing the passing of Measure B, or the San Diego County Health & Safety Act, after last week’s election at the San Diego County Administration Building on Monday, Nov. 9, 2026. / Vito Di Stefano for Voice of San Diego 
 This week on the Voice of San Diego podcast, Supervisor Terra Lawson-Remer sat down with Scott Lewis and Andrea Sanchez-Villafaña. 
 Lawson-Remer brought a surfboard to Voice’s podcast studios — fresh off a voter-approved sales tax that would partially fund cleaning up the Tijuana River sewage crisis. She and Voice CEO Scott Lewis have pledged to surf Imperial Beach 10 years from now. 
 Despite polls showing voters felt the county was heading in the wrong direction, they voted to give county officials billions in new revenue and a whole lot more power. The trio broke down the A’s and B’s of Measures A and B that appeared on this year’s ballot. 
 Listen to the full episode here. 
 Sacramento Report: California’s Bluest Wave Yet  
 In surf terms, the midterms delivered California Democrats a clean-up set. The Golden State’s blue wave was so large, it washed out any chance at Republican power, clinching a historic Democratic supermajority in the state Legislature. Democrats will outnumber Republicans 120-19, writes our Nadia Lathan. 
 What will Democrats do with all that power? 
 They hope to restore medical care for noncitizens that was stripped from this year’s budget, reform CARE court rules and wildfire liability and more. 
 Read the full Sacramento Report here. 
 In Other News 
 Flights at the San Diego International Airport were delayed as the FAA experienced country-wide grounding of planes. (CBS 8)
 An elephant died at the San Diego Zoo last week and now another one is sick. (City News Service) 
 The city of El Cajon remains a GOP stronghold , reports the Union-Tribune. Republican Mayor Bill Wells won re-election after facing a Democratic Socialist challenger. 
 Crowds gathered at different San Diego beaches this weekend to watch the huge and dramatic waves brought on by Pacific storms. (NBC 7 San Diego)  
 The Morning Report was written by MacKenzie Elmer and Jakob McWhinney. It was edited by Will Huntsberry and Andrea Sanchez-Villafaña.
